title: The pot and the lid
hook: like a water pot turned upside down, nothing stays in; an upright pot fills

segments.voice: Yesterday: ahara, food, and the desert travelers who ate only to cross. Your line: just enough to cross.

How much of this week stayed with you? Girimananda's bedside. The nuns and the inspiring sign. Six ways to be dear. The old Buddha in the evening sun. Seven marks of a friend. The desert crossing. That's a lot of teaching in seven days. The Book of Threes has a sutta for exactly this question. It sorts listeners into three kinds, with three homely pictures: a pot turned upside down, a lap full of snacks, and a pot standing the right way up.
screen: `HOW MUCH STAYED?` → `A WEEK OF TEACHINGS.` → `THREE KINDS OF LISTENER.`

segments.voice: The first listener goes often to hear the teaching, and it's good in the beginning, middle and end. But they don't attend to any of it, not while sitting, not after they get up. That person, the Buddha says, is like a pot turned upside down. Pour water on it, and it all runs off. The second listener follows while sitting, beginning, middle and end. But once they stand up, it's gone, like a person with sesame seeds and rice cakes in their lap who forgets and stands up, and everything scatters on the ground. The third listener takes it in while sitting and still holds it after getting up: a pot standing upright. Pour water in, and it stays. About today's title: there's no lid in the sutta. There's an upside-down pot, a lap and an upright pot. The lid is my word, and a fair one. Plenty of people listen with a lid on: the phone in one hand, the reply already half-composed. Notice that the first two listeners aren't lazy. They show up and sit through the whole thing. The difference is the angle of the pot. Turning it upright is something you can do: recall a teaching later, repeat it to someone, try it once.
screen: `THE UPSIDE-DOWN POT.` · `THE LAP THAT SPILLS.` · `THE UPRIGHT POT.` · then, large: `KEEP THE POT UPRIGHT.`

segments.voice: Picture a clay pot resting in your lap, mouth up, and let this week's lines pour in, one at a time: ten perceptions; inspired, then calm; six ways to be dear; even his; a friend gives the hard thing; just enough to cross. Notice which ones stayed in and which ran off, with no grading. Then hold the one that matters most to you for a few breaths.
avakujja. The Pali word for upside down, naming the first of three listeners in the Book of Threes: an upside-down pot, a spilling lap, and an upright pot that holds what's poured in. Today's word.
Your line: keep the pot upright. What's poured in can stay. Day six hundred seventy-nine, done.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers sometimes use the three pots when encouraging students to review and practice what they hear, and in some communities Dhamma talks are followed by recitation or discussion to help the teaching stay.

chat.says: You went to that talk. Does it matter if you forget it all afterward?
options: Yes: hearing it isn't the same as holding it, like an upright pot.
No: the sutta says forgetting is fine as long as you showed up.
Only if you were lazy; the spilling listeners never showed up.
chat.meaning: In the Book of Threes, the first two listeners do show up, but only the upright pot holds what's poured in.

notes: AN 3.30 paraphrased. Confirm the lap items (sesame, rice, sweets/cakes) and the 'wide wisdom' (puthu-panna) naming.
